s.def: Describing an illegal and intentional act that is nevertheless not blameworthy, for example because its positive consequences outweighed the bad. Distinguished from excusable, describing an involuntary illegal act.
ex: justifiable homicide

ety: From Middle English justificacioun, justification, from Middle French justification, from Late Latin iustificationem, justificationem < iustificatio, from iustifico, from Latin iustus.

s.def: A reason, explanation, or excuse which someone believes provides convincing, morally acceptable support for behavior or for a belief or occurrence.
The forgiveness of sin.
ex: […] to articulate a common understanding of our justification by God’s grace through faith in Christ.

s.def: The alignment of text to the left margin (left justification), the right margin (right justification), or both margins (full justification).

ety: From Middle English justifien, from Old French justifier, from Late Latin justificare (“make just”), from Latin justus, iustus (“just”) + ficare (“make”), from facere, equivalent to just + -ify.

s.def: To provide an acceptable explanation for.
ex: How can you justify spending so much money on clothes?
Paying too much for car insurance is not justified.

s.def: To be a good reason behind a normally-unacceptable action; to warrant.
ex: Nothing can justify your rude behaviour last night.
Preservation of two railway routes between Belfast and Derry could no longer be justified and one of them must go.

s.def: To arrange (text) on a page or a computer screen such that the left and right ends of all lines within paragraphs are aligned.
ex: The text will look better justified.

s.def: To absolve, and declare to be free of blame or sin.
ex: I cannot justify whom the law condemns.
And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.

s.def: To give reasons for one’s actions; to make an argument to prove that one is in the right.
ex: She felt no need to justify herself for deciding not to invite him.
[…] I was equally unable to justify myself and unwilling to acknowledge my errors […]

s.def: To prove; to ratify; to confirm.
ex: […] say My wife’s a hobby-horse, deserves a name As rank as any flax-wench that puts to Before her troth-plight: say’t and justify’t.

s.def: To show (a person) to have had a sufficient legal reason for an act that has been made the subject of a charge or accusation.
To qualify (oneself) as a surety by taking oath to the ownership of sufficient property.
ex: J'USTIFYING BAIL, practice, is the production of bail in court, who there justify' themselves against the exception of the plaintiff.

ety: From Middle English jutten (“to project, jut out”), an alteration of jetten (“to strut, be showy”). More at English jet.

s.def: To stick out.
ex: the jutting part of a building
1725-1726, William Broome, The Odyssey It seems to jut out of the structure of the poem.
...enormous Chesterfield packs aslant on the scoreboards, a couple of cigarettes jutting from each.

s.def: To butt.
ex: 1772-1782, William Mason, The English Garden the jutting steer

s.def: Something that sticks out.

ety: Borrowed from Bengali ঝুট (jhuṭ). Likely related to Ukrainian джгут (džhut) and Russian жгут (žgut).

s.def: The coarse, strong fibre of the East Indian plants, Corchorus olitorius and Corchorus capsularis, used to make mats, paper, gunny cloth etc.
The plants from which this fibre is obtained.

ety: From Latin plural Iuti, Iutae (in Bede), from Old English Ēotas. Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *eut, from Proto-Germanic *eutaz, *eutaniz. The spelling was later influenced by Medieval Latin Jutae, Juti.

s.def: A member of the Germanic tribe that existed in modern-day Denmark that invaded England about the same time as the Angles and the Saxons in the beginning of the Middle Ages, but were eventually integrated by the time of the Norman Conquest.
ex: No Jute is left to wield a sword to save this hoard. No one is left to swing the battle-ax skyward.

s.def: An annual herb (Corchorus olitorius) in the family Malvaceae, cultivated as a source of jute fibre.

ety: See Jute.

s.def: A cultural region and peninsula in northwestern Europe, consisting of the mainland part of Denmark and Schleswig-Holstein, which is part of Germany.

ety: From Latin juvenescens, present participle of juvenesco; by surface analysis, juven(ile) + -escent.

s.def: Especially of one's mind or spirit, becoming juvenile or young.
Catachresis for juvenile.

ety: Borrowed from Latin iuvenīlis (“youthful; juvenile”), from iuvenis (“young; a youth”) + -īlis (suffix forming adjectives indicating a relationship or a pertaining to). Iuvenis is ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁en- (“young”), from *h₂óyu (“long life; lifetime”) (from *h₂ey- (“age; life”)) + *h₁én (“in”).

s.def: Young; not fully developed.
Characteristic of youth or immaturity; childish.
ex: He indicated that Cheong should follow his actions, but Cheong was little tempted and chose not to engage in such a juvenile scene.

s.def: A prepubescent child.
A person younger than the age of majority; a minor.
A person younger than the age of full criminal responsibility, such that the person either cannot be held criminally liable or is subject to less severe forms of punishment.
A publication for young adult readers.
ex: Formerly a publisher of juveniles, out of the market till 1959, when it will enter adult fiction field.

s.def: An actor playing a child's role.
A sexually immature animal.
A two-year-old racehorse.
ex: Even more incredible is the legion of two-year-olds who win handsomely as juveniles and then disappear from the racetrack.

s.def: Participation in illegal behaviour by minors.

ety: From Latin iuvenīlia, neuter plural of iuvenīlis (“of or pertaining to youth”). By surface analysis, juvenile + -ia

s.def: Works produced during an artist's or author's youth.
ex: Lewis’s juvenilia is childlike, and the way it has been handled is childish.

ety: Borrowed from Latin iuvenilitas. By surface analysis, juvenile + -ity.

s.def: The state or quality of being juvenile.
ex: The plant grew from juvenility to maturity in a week.
Next in juvenility to Abraham came two more girls, Hope and Modesty; then a boy of three, and then the baby, who had just completed his first year.

s.def: Juvenile behavior, writing, etc.
ex: The frantic fanaticism of this paragraph deprives us of all hope that Mr. Irving will, as we once fondly hoped, outgrow his juvenilities.

ety: Borrowed from French juxtaposer, corresponding to juxta- + pose, derived from Latin iuxtā (“near, next to”) + pōnō (“place”).

s.def: To place side by side, especially for contrast or comparison.
ex: The artist used contrasting colors to juxtapose light and dark.
The documentary effectively juxtaposes the lives of two rival politicians.
In the study, they juxtaposed economic growth with social welfare indicators.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from Arabic جُزْء (juzʔ).

s.def: Any of thirty parts of varying length into which the Qur'an is sometimes divided.
